title: Infra Team Wiki: GPU Fleet, Cloud Accounts, IaC Modules, CI/CD & Runbooks (Playbook)
author: Ethan Chen
body:
Overview

This playbook consolidates infrastructure engineering guidance for the GPU fleet, capacity planning, cloud account and networking patterns, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD and build pipelines, and runbooks used day-to-day by the infra team. It is intended as the canonical team wiki reference for new hires and on-call engineers.

Scope

- GPU fleet provisioning and capacity management for Redwood Inference hosted and dedicated environments.
- Cloud account organization, VPC/networking baselines, and peering/egress rules.
- Terraform & IaC module catalog, conventions, and release guidance.
- CI/CD pipelines for infra modules and GPU node images.
- Runbooks for common incidents (capacity shortage, node failures, networking faults).

Ownership and Contacts

- Primary owner: infra-gpu-platform (team alias)
- Secondary owner: eng-infra-networking
- Pager: infra-oncall (rotates weekly)
- Slack channels: #infra-gpu, #infra-deploys, #sre-oncall

Service-level objectives (SLOs) & Key Metrics

- GPU request admission latency: 99th percentile < 150ms (control plane only)
- Node replacement time (detected failure -> ready replacement): P95 < 6 minutes
- Autoscaling reaction time (scale up for sustained 60s over threshold): P95 < 90s
- Cost per effective GPU-hour tracked weekly vs budget target

Architecture summary

- GPU nodes run in dedicated worker pools per environment: hosted, dedicated, private-customer (VPC).
- Each pool is backed by a managed instance group (MIG / ASG) or Kubernetes nodegroup depending on deployment target.
- A placement controller routes model-serving workloads by model family and latency tier to compatible instance types (e.g., A100, H100, L4).
- Caching & batching layer sits in front of the fleet to reduce token compute; autoscaler considers effective CPU/GPU utilization after batching.

Terraform / IaC Modules (catalog and conventions)

We maintain a centralized modules registry in the infra-iac GitHub org. Naming convention: tf-mod-<area>-<purpose>. Module args follow a common pattern (env, name_prefix, tags, owner_team).

Table: core modules

module_name | repo | primary_vars | owner_team
---------|-------|----------------|----------
tf-mod-gpu-nodegroup | github.com/redwood/infra-iac/tf-mod-gpu-nodegroup | instance_type, desired_capacity, gpu_profile | engineering
tf-mod-vpc-baseline | github.com/redwood/infra-iac/tf-mod-vpc-baseline | cidr_block, private_subnets, nat_config | engineering
tf-mod-iam-roles | github.com/redwood/infra-iac/tf-mod-iam-roles | role_map, trust_accounts | security
tf-mod-network-peering | github.com/redwood/infra-iac/tf-mod-network-peering | peer_account, peer_vpc, allowed_cidrs | engineering
tf-mod-image-build | github.com/redwood/infra-iac/tf-mod-image-build | image_name, build_args | engineering

Module authoring guidelines

- Modules must be small, composable, and idempotent. Aim for 20-200 LOC per module.
- Inputs: explicit, typed, with defaults for non-sensitive values.
- Outputs: minimal (ids, names, ARNs). Use consistent naming keys: resource_name, resource_id, arn.
- Ownership: add owner_tag and a CODEOWNERS entry pointing to owner_team.
- Tests: every module requires at least one unit test (terratest) and a smoke deploy pipeline.

CI/CD and build pipelines

Pipeline patterns

- Module PRs: Validate -> Plan -> Apply (apply to a sandbox env only on merge to main).
- Release flow: tag module release via git tag, publish module documentation site, update dependent stacks via automated PRs.
- Image builds: use buildkite pipeline infra-image-build -> push to private container registry -> image-scanning -> sign artifact.
- Promotion: sandbox -> staging -> prod using IaC variable overrides and controlled merge gates.

Example pipeline steps (module PR)

1. Run fmt & validate (terraform fmt, tflint, checkov).
2. Run terratest unit tests (parallelizable).
3. Generate terraform plan (planfile) and upload to PR.
4. On approval, merge triggers CI job that runs apply against the sandbox workspace.
5. Automated smoke test validates resource availability; failures trigger rollback and pager.

Secrets, CI tokens and policy

- CI jobs must use short-lived, scoped credentials from the centralized CI-oauth service. Avoid long-lived machine credentials in pipelines.
- Terraform state is stored in remote state backends (S3 + DynamoDB for locking or equivalent) with encryption at rest and bucket policies limiting write access to the infra service account.

Cloud accounts and networking baseline

Account structure

- Root org: redwood-cloud-org. Accounts: management, security, prod-hosted, prod-dedicated, sandbox-<team>.
- Account ownership and billing tags are required on all resources.

Networking design

- VPC baseline uses three AZs where available with the following subnets: public, private-app, private-management.
- Default egress controlled via NAT gateway or egress-only NAT for IPv6.
- Centralized shared services VPC hosts logging, tracer, and artifact proxies; peering / Transit Gateway for cross-account connectivity.

Security & firewall rules

- Node egress: restrict to internal endpoints and approved registries.
- Control plane (placement, autoscaler, admission) runs in a hardened management VPC and communicates to worker pools over explicit peered connections.
- All SSH access is disabled; operational access via jumpbox bastion with short-lived certs and session recording.

GPU fleet & capacity planning

Capacity model

- Track two capacity dimensions: reserved capacity (for Dedicated customers) and dynamic capacity (for hosted workloads).
- Maintain buffer headroom target: 15% of total available GPU-hours in each region during business hours as warm pool for burst.
- Weekly capacity forecast: based on 7/14/30 day rolling usage and active customer rollouts.

Instance types and profiles

- Profiles:
  - high-performance (H100/A100): latency-sensitive model families
  - cost-optimized (L4, T4x): inference for small models and embeddings
  - memory-optimized: large context models with high VRAM

Allocation & placement policies

- Placement controller uses affinity rules to keep warm pools for high-tier customers pinned to reserved capacity.
- Low-priority jobs (batch evals, QA) are preemptible and scheduled on spare capacity.

Autoscaling rules (example)

- Scale-up trigger: sustained GPU utilization > 70% for 60s AND queue_length > 5 pending pods -> +1 node group increment.
- Scale-down trigger: sustained GPU utilization < 25% for 300s AND no pending high-priority pods -> -1 node group decrement (respect min_size).
- Cooldown: 120s between sequential scale events.

Runbooks (high priority)

1) Capacity shortage (high severity)

- Symptoms: queuing requests, increased 5xx from scheduler, alert: gpu_fleet_pending_queue_p95 > 30s.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Acknowledge pager and create incident channel (Zoom + #incident-infra).
  2. Check autoscaler logs and recent scale events: infra-monitoring -> dashboards -> GPU Fleet -> Scaling history.
  3. Manually increase nodegroup desired_capacity by +20% for affected region using the ramp command: 
     - CLI example (GCP): gcloud compute instance-groups managed resize <group> --size=<new_size> --zone=<zone>
     - Terraform quick fix (temporary): terraform workspace select prod && terraform apply -var 'override_desired=<new_size>' -target=module.tf-mod-gpu-nodegroup
  4. Verify new nodes register and pods schedule (kubectl get nodes; kubectl describe pods -n redwood-serving).
  5. If nodes fail to come up, check image build registry, subnet IP exhaustion, and account quota.

2) Node failure / OOMs

- Symptoms: high node-restart-rate, GPU OOM events in node logs.
- Steps:
  1. Drain node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data.
  2. Inspect node logs (journalctl / cloud provider logs) and report to hardware team if recurrent.
  3. Replace node via instance group managed recreate or delete; ensure autoscaler triggers new instance.

3) Networking outage to shared services

- Symptoms: control plane errors, inability to reach artifact registry or secret store.
- Steps:
  1. Confirm route table changes or peering state.
  2. Failover to alternate egress (preconfigured NAT or egress proxy).
  3. For long outages, re-route critical traffic via Transit Gateway or VPC peering fallback.

Operational tooling & dashboards

Key dashboards and alerts

- GPU Fleet Overview: utilization, queue length, per-region headroom. Alert: gpu_fleet_headroom_percent < 12%
- Node Health: node_restarts_5m > 5 per nodegroup -> P1 alert
- Autoscaler Failures: autoscaler_sync_errors > 0 -> P1 if > 5 in 10m
- Image build pipeline: last_successful_build_age > 24h -> P2

Common CLI & diagnostic commands

- kubectl get pods -A -o wide --selector=app=redwood-serving
- kubectl top nodes --heapster
- aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=tag:Name,Values=redwood-gpu*"
- gcloud compute instances list --filter="name~'^redwood-gpu'"

Checklist: releasing a new GPU node image

1. Build image pipeline: infra-image-build (Buildkite) -> push to registry.
2. Run image-scan and sign artifact.
3. Create canary nodegroup with image tag <image>:canary in sandbox.
4. Smoke test: run synthetic inference load for 30m, verify latency & mem.
5. Promote image to staging -> repeat smoke tests.
6. Rollout to prod via canary deploy (10% -> 50% -> 100%) with rollback job if <quality metrics.

FAQ and troubleshooting tips

- Q: Who can approve changes to reserved capacity?
  A: Only infra-gpu-platform leads and finance-approved capacity managers.
- Q: What to do if Terraform plan shows drift?
  A: Investigate remote state vs real resources, check for manual changes, run terraform refresh in a sandbox and open a drift ticket.

Appendix: example terraform snippet (nodegroup)

module "gpu_nodegroup" {
  source = "github.com/redwood/infra-iac//tf-mod-gpu-nodegroup"
  env = "prod"
  name_prefix = "redwood-gpu-h100"
  instance_type = "nvidia-h100"
  desired_capacity = 20
  min_size = 4
  max_size = 80
  tags = { team = "infra-gpu", owner = "infra-gpu-platform" }
}

Document maintenance

- Owner must review this page quarterly or after any significant architecture change.
- Major changes require reviewer approvals listed above and an update to related runbooks.

Links & references

- infra-iac repo: github.com/redwood/infra-iac
- GPU capacity runbook (detailed): eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026.json
- Module registry & docs: internal-docs/modules-site

End of playbook
